verdicts.issue: Source is a conditional prayer: 'if you heard me when I prayed to you aforetime, and did me honour while you sent disaster on the Achaeans, vouchsafe me now the fulfilment of yet this further prayer'. AFTER turns it into assertions ('you heard me ... and honored me by sending disaster... Now grant me') and loses the 'if'.
verdicts.fix: In front of them all, two men armed themselves—Patroclus and Automedon—two men with one mind, to lead the Myrmidons. Then Achilles went into his tent and opened the lid of the strong chest that silver-footed Thetis had given him to take on board ship, and had filled with shirts, cloaks against the cold, and good thick rugs. In this chest he kept a cup of rare workmanship. No man but himself might drink from it, and he made offerings from it to no god except father Zeus. He took the cup from the chest and cleansed it with sulphur. Then he rinsed it in clean water, washed his hands, and drew wine. He stood in the middle of the court and prayed, looking toward heaven and pouring out the wine as a drink offering. Zeus, whose joy is in thunder, did not fail to see him. “King Zeus,” he cried, “lord of Dodona, god of the Pelasgi, you who live far away and rule wintry Dodona, where your prophets the Selli live around you with unwashed feet and beds made on the ground—if you heard me when I prayed to you before, and honored me by sending disaster on the Achaeans, grant me now the fulfillment of one more prayer. I will stay here where my ships are lying, but I am sending my comrade into battle at the head of many Myrmidons. Grant, all-seeing Zeus, that victory goes with him. Put your courage into his heart, so that Hector learns whether my squire is man enough to fight alone, or whether his might is unbeatable only when I myself enter the turmoil of war. Afterward, when he has driven the fighting and the battle cry away from the ships, grant that he returns unharmed, with his armor and his comrades, fighters in close combat.”

verdicts.issue: Source: 'he first took it to a place where Priam should not see it'. AFTER adds 'himself', emphasis the source does not state.
verdicts.fix: The old man was afraid of him and obeyed. Then the son of Peleus sprang out through the door of his house like a lion. He did not go alone. His two squires, Automedon and Alcimus, went with him. Now that Patroclus was dead, he valued these two above all his other comrades. They unyoked the horses and mules, and told Priam’s herald and attendant to sit inside the house. They lifted the ransom for Hector’s body down from the wagon, but left two mantles and a fine shirt for Achilles to wrap the body in when it was given back to be taken home. Then Achilles called to his servants and told them to wash the body and anoint it. First he took it to a place where Priam could not see it. He was afraid that Priam, seeing it, might break out in the bitterness of his grief and enrage him, so that he would kill the old man and sin against the word of Zeus. When the servants had washed and anointed the body and wrapped it in a fair shirt and mantle, Achilles himself lifted it onto a bier, and he and his men laid it on the wagon. As he did so he cried aloud and called on his dear comrade by name. “Do not be angry with me, Patroclus,” he said, “if you learn, even in the house of Hades, that I gave Hector back to his father for a ransom. It was not an unworthy one, and I will share it with you fairly.”
